newsitem.title: USA: Dole steps up push for California votes.
newsitem.headline: Dole steps up push for California votes.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole on Sunday stepped up his attacks on illegal immigration and affirmative action in California trying to cut President Bill Clinton's commanding lead in the prize state.

At a rally of Vietnamese-Americans, Dole said Clinton had not done enough to police the nation's borders and reiterated his support for a controverisal ballot initative here to end affirmative action and preferences in government hiring, contracting and school admissions.

Dole aides said the Kansas Republican, who has extended his Californian trip by one day, plans major speeches on the two issues on Monday and Tuesday. Clinton opposes the Californian affirmative action initiative.

"There are no limits on what individuals can achieve in this country when they come here as legal immigrants. Because in America what counts is merit and character," Dole said standing before a red, white and blue banner that read "Celebrating Legal Immigration, the American Dream."

"Quotas, set asides and other preferences that discriminate by race or ethnicity are simply wrong in America ... and do violence to the principles of our Constitution," Dole said. Speaking to voters after the event, he called affirmative action and immigration "wedge issues."

Dole has decided to focus much of his time and resources in California in the closing days of the campaign. The state has 54 of the 270 electoral college votes needed to win the presidency on the Nov 5 Election Day.
Dole said he was pleased by Reform Party candidate Ross Perot's comments on Sunday, in which the Texas billionaire said Dole would be a better military commander-in-chief than Clinton.

Perot, on NBC-TV's "Meet the Press", said, "Senator Dole understands combat. He has certainly paid a terrible price, and if you were limited to those too, you'd certainly, I think every American would pick him, because he understands what he's doing. The other candidate (Clinton), has no experience in military or in combat."

Dole campaign manager Scott Reed traveled to Dallas last week to try to persuade Perot to drop his third-party candidacy in the hope that Perot supporters might move into Dole's column. Perot turned Dole down, but has since attacked the ethics of the Clinton administration.
"I think he's (Perot) being very positive in telling the American people they have a choice and I'm the better choice," Dole said.

During the rally Dole also complained about the New York Times decision to endorse Clinton. Dole has attacked what he calls the "liberal media" during the past week. The crowd booed reporters after Dole egged them on.
Dole had based his decision to focus on California on a poll showing him closing the gap with Clinton. But a Los Angeles Times survey last week showed Clinton 20 points ahead of Dole in the state.
His campaign plans to focus heavily on immigration. Half of Dole's television ads here and all of his radio ads will be on that single issue.

"Thousands of Californians have been victims of violent criminals who should have been stopped at the borders before they ever set foot in America," Dole said. "That is a price that people pay for the federal government's failure to secure the border."
California voters by a wide margin passed an initiative to bar most benefits to illegal immigrants, but it has been held up by the courts.
Dole once again attacked the White House for a long list of ethics scandals, including Whitewater.

But in front of the ethnic crowd, he did not repeat his call to bar noncitizens from contributing to political campaigns. Dole also did not attack the White House for rushing the citizenship applications of legal immigrants, as he has in recent days.
During the last session of Congress, lawmakers voted to bar legal immigrants from receiving many federal services. Dole supported that legislation.
Clinton has invested much time and effort trying to woo California, visiting the state nearly 30 times since his election and dispensing federal defense contracts and other government benefits.
